doc.title: Darius Brubeck interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 29, 2024

title: Mamazala, Zim Ngqawana and mbaqanga
summary: The piece by his student Zim Ngqawana blends church harmony with a slowed Confirmation; mbaqanga described.

story.theme_name: Church, faith and religion in a musician's life
story.community_name: Church, faith and jazz: the sacred and the secular

blocks.x: Okay, well speaking of impacted, I wanted to talk about your own composition process, and earlier today I listened to your quartet, this goes back to a concert at Queens Hall in Edinburgh, and “Mamazada”?

“Mamazala.” I got this feeling that it was a combination of church music, blues, and some classical and some South African thing in there. And I’m wondering how that particular piece came to be and if it’s a model for how you usually work?

Well everything you’ve said about it is true but it’s not a model for me because it was composed by one of my former students who was also in the Jazzanians and his name is Zim Ngqawana. And you’ll find his name on the album and in the book so you’ll be able to spell it. But you’re very correct, the kind of piano voicings in the head are just church. And that comes from the tradition Christian missionaries introduced that kind of harmony in choral singing and Africans really excel at that. Again, they’re not reading, they just know that young men have higher voices than older men and women have higher voices still, and they do four part like, you know, it’s like magic really that it sounds so good. And the piano does the same kind of thing. But the improv section if you analyze it is actually “Confirmation” slowed down. So that’s the jazz bit and the joke that the African musicians had about that particular piece, which is quite popular, is they called it “ECM Mbaqanga.”
ECM as in the record label?
Okay, followed by what was that you said?

Mbaqanga. It’s kind of their blues form. It’s their roots music which has a very predictable kind of harmonic, you know, chordal progression and it can go on infinitely like a blues with variations like the blues but always the same kind of harmonic cycle, open endedly you know for exposition and then someone says, “Oh it’s time to play the head again” and they do. But it can be very arranged or not arranged at all, but yeah, just think of it as like the blues but for South Africans.
